what: Wrong NIV threshold: the right-answer text says "pH below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 after optimal medical treatment: BTS/ICS criteria for NIV". BTS/ICS 2016 uses PaCO2 > 6.5 kPa (about 49 mmHg), not 45. MRCEM candidates are examined on this number.
evidence: Davidson AC et al. BTS/ICS guideline for ventilatory management of AHRF, Thorax 2016;71 Suppl 2 (NIV when pH <7.35 and PaCO2 >6.5 kPa persist despite optimal medical therapy).
fix: Change to: "pH below 7.35 and PaCO2 above 6.5 kPa (about 49 mmHg) persisting after optimal medical treatment: BTS/ICS criteria for NIV. pH below 7.26 means a higher risk of failure: start it in a place where it can be escalated (HDU), with a ceiling-of-care decision."

what: The gas (pH 7.47, PCO2 22, HCO3 15.6) fits the CHRONIC respiratory alkalosis rule almost exactly (expected HCO3 = 24 - 5 x 1.8 = 15). The app's own interpreter, opened on the same values, says "Primary respiratory alkalosis - Chronic, renally compensated" plus HAGMA. The case explanation never says why compensation is not the answer, so a learner applying the app's rules gets a contradiction.
evidence: interp(CASES ch-asa step 0 gas): compensation step => "Chronic, renally compensated :: Acute: HCO3 ~ 20.4; chronic: ~ 15. Measured 15.6"; gaps => AG 21.4.
fix: Add to the right-answer text: "Six hours is too soon for renal compensation: the acute rule predicts HCO3 ~ 20; 15.6 with an anion gap of 21 is a second, metabolic process." Optionally lower HCO3 to ~13.5 and PCO2 to ~19 (pH 7.47) so the numbers do not sit on the chronic line.

where: ch-dka step 3 (potassium) option "Hold insulin until potassium is normal"
what: Feedback "Potassium 5.6 is not a reason to delay insulin; below 3.5 is" is imprecise. JBDS 2023 does not tell you to hold the FRIII at <3.5: it asks for senior review and extra potassium; the ADA threshold for delaying insulin is K <3.3. Learners will carry "hold insulin below 3.5" into exams.
evidence: JBDS 02 single-page pathway, March 2023 (K bands >5.5 / 3.5-5.5 / <3.5 senior review); ADA hyperglycaemic crises consensus 2024 (hold insulin if K <3.3).
fix: Rewrite: "A high potassium is not a reason to delay insulin. Only a low one changes the plan: below 3.5 JBDS asks for senior review and more potassium (ADA delays insulin until K is above 3.3)."

what: The message gives chloride 112 and asks the learner to see that "the gap is closing" but gives no sodium, so the anion gap cannot be calculated. It also says "add 10% glucose once glucose is below 14 mmol/L" when glucose is already 12, so the drip should already be running.
evidence: c12.js line 11: m: "glucose 12, ketones 1.4, pH 7.24, HCO3 14, chloride 112" - no Na; right-answer text: "add 10% glucose once glucose is below 14".
fix: Add "sodium 138" (AG = 138 - 112 - 14 = 12) and reword: "...Keep the fixed-rate insulin running (JBDS 2023: consider dropping to 0.05 units/kg/h), and the 10% glucose at 125 mL/h should already be running since glucose fell below 14. Follow ketones and pH, not bicarbonate: chloride keeps the bicarbonate low."

where: im-capno steps 1–3, im-dip step 1, im-print A/B, im-syringe step 2 (question text)
what: Image-led stems describe the image in words, so the image is never needed: 'the upstroke is slow and sloping, like a shark fin', 'a notch (cleft) appears in the plateau', 'Dipstick: blood +++', 'PO₂ 38, PCO₂ 48'. The format exists to train reading the picture.
evidence: Read any step of im-capno: answer is derivable from the stem alone.
fix: Neutral stems: 'Trace 1. What is the most likely cause?', 'Read the strip against the microscopy: 0–2 RBC/hpf. Why the mismatch?', 'Printout B is labelled arterial. Can you trust it?' Keep the description in the explanation instead.

what: Shown as an analyser printout, but analysers CALCULATE cHCO₃⁻ from pH and PCO₂ (the printout even shows the 'c' suffix: 'cHCO₃⁻(P)c'). A real printout cannot fail the Henderson check; only a transcription, or pH/PCO₂ from the gas set beside a chemistry-lab bicarbonate (total CO₂) from another time, can. Teaches a wrong model of the analyser.
evidence: Screenshot /tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/80312b5f-0e45-5589-b131-fcf824f33899/scratchpad/beta/shots/T21-im-print-s1-390-dark.png. AARC 2013 (hemoximetry/analysis: HCO₃⁻ is calculated).
fix: Recast A as a handwritten ward chart / a nurse's typed results message (pH, PCO₂ from the gas; HCO₃⁻ 14 from the lab sheet), not a printout; explanation: 'the analyser calculates HCO₃⁻ from pH and PCO₂, so a mismatch means a transcription error or numbers from different samples/times'. Needs a new img type (e.g. 'note') in ui8.js.

what: The case data has no debrief teaching content (no learning points, no exam pearls), so caseEnd() cannot show any.
evidence: grep of c12.js: fields are id, fmt, t, pres, dis, set, exam, src, steps; there is no learning-point field.
fix: Add learn:[…3 short points…] and pearl:'…' to each case (16 cases).

what: "Very high levels and new neurological signs point to haemodialysis": 720 mg/L (5.2 mmol/L) is not "very high" by EXTRIP (ECTR recommended above 7.2 mmol/L / 1000 mg/L, or 6.5 with impaired kidneys). The real trigger here is altered mental status (agitation), which is an EXTRIP indication at any level. UK TOXBASE uses >700 mg/L, which is why 720 was likely chosen; neither threshold is named.
evidence: Juurlink DN et al. EXTRIP salicylate recommendations, Ann Emerg Med 2015;66:165-181.
fix: Rewrite: "Agitation is altered mental status: EXTRIP recommends haemodialysis whatever the level (level alone: above 7.2 mmol/L; UK TOXBASE uses above 700 mg/L). Alkalinise meanwhile (target urine pH 7.5-8.5), keep K+ above 4, and give glucose: the brain can be hypoglycaemic with a normal blood glucose."

what: Inconsistent Winter's numbers. The right answer says "1.5 x 5.6 + 8 = 16 ± 2; the venous 19 matches an arterial ~14-17"; the distractor says "band is about 14-18". The app standard converts venous HCO3 -1 too, so the interpreter gives 1.5 x 4.6 + 8 = 14.9 ± 2 (13-17) and AG 30.4 (29.9 albumin-corrected) vs the case's 29.
evidence: interp(ch-dka gas): "Winter's: 1.5 x 4.6 + 8 = 14.9 ± 2 -> expected PCO2 13-17 mmHg. Measured 14"; AG 30.4.
fix: Use one set of numbers in both texts, matching the app's venous->arterial rule: "Estimated arterial HCO3 ~4.6, PCO2 ~14; Winter's 1.5 x 4.6 + 8 = 15 ± 2 (13-17): appropriate. AG ~ 30."

what: The case never says this is SEVERE DKA, though it meets three JBDS severity markers: HR 124 (>100), AG ~29 (>16), and estimated arterial HCO3 4.6 (<5). In JBDS these trigger senior review and HDU/level-2 care, a standard MRCEM question.
evidence: JBDS 02 (2023) severity criteria: ketones >6, HCO3 <5, venous pH <7.0, K <3.5 on admission, GCS <12, SpO2 <92%, SBP <90, HR >100 or <60, AG >16.
fix: Add a line to step 2's right answer ("This meets JBDS severity criteria: HR >100, AG >16, bicarbonate about 5: call the senior and plan HDU") or add a short step "Where should she be managed?".

what: The plan leaves out oxygen targets and leans on CPAP. For a probable OHS patient with acute hypercapnia, BTS 2017 sets SpO2 88-92%, and bilevel NIV (not CPAP) is the treatment for acute hypercapnia. Opioid-sparing analgesia and HDU/level-2 monitoring are also missing. The ATS 2019 point that serum HCO3 >= 27 is the screening trigger, which fits this gas (32), is not taught.
evidence: Mokhlesi B et al. ATS OHS guideline 2019 (HCO3 <27 makes OHS unlikely; suspected OHS discharged on NIV until outpatient work-up); O'Driscoll BR et al. BTS oxygen 2017 (target 88-92% in obesity hypoventilation).
fix: Right answer: "HDU-level monitoring, titrate oxygen to 88-92%, bilevel NIV overnight, consider a naloxone infusion, switch to opioid-sparing analgesia, and refer for OHS work-up (HCO3 32 >= 27, the ATS screening trigger)."

where: ch-pca step 2 distractor "Pure acute respiratory acidosis with no background"
what: Feedback "The bicarbonate is a little higher than acute alone predicts" undersells it: 32 vs about 27 is 5 mmol/L, well outside the acute range. The right answer also does not mention the other cause of a value between the two lines (acute respiratory acidosis plus a metabolic alkalosis, e.g. post-op vomiting or diuretics).
evidence: Acute: 24 + 3.4 = 27.4; chronic: 24 + 13.6 = 37.6; measured 32 (interp agrees).
fix: Change to "HCO3 32 is about 5 above the acute prediction (~27): there is a background of retention." Add to the right answer: "...or an added metabolic alkalosis; the history (BMI 44, sleepy by day) favours chronic retention."

what: The calculated osmolality "2 x Na + glucose + urea = 293" implies a urea of 5 that is never given, and ethanol ("low" but measured) is left out of the formula, so learners cannot reproduce the 293 or learn to subtract the ethanol share.
evidence: 2 x 141 + 6 = 288, so urea must be 5 for 293. Intro: "Ethanol level is low".
fix: Give urea 5.0 in the message and either say "ethanol undetectable" in the intro or include it: "2 x Na + glucose + urea + ethanol (mmol/L) = 293".

what: Treatment is incomplete for an MRCEM learner. It does not give the EXTRIP dialysis criteria that this patient meets (visual signs, AG >24, pH <= 7.15), and leaves out the adjuncts: bicarbonate to keep pH above 7.3 and folinic/folic acid to clear formate.
evidence: Roberts DM et al. EXTRIP methanol recommendations, Crit Care Med 2015;43:461-472; Kraut & Mullins NEJM 2018.
fix: Extend: "...dialysis is indicated: visual signs, anion gap above 24 and pH 7.15 or less all meet EXTRIP criteria. Add bicarbonate (target pH above 7.3) and folinic acid."

what: Explanation cites only ACOG 2006 (Committee Opinion 348). It misses the practical next step that the user's ER/UK context needs: pH < 7.00 within 60 min meets criterion A for therapeutic hypothermia, so the baby needs a structured encephalopathy exam (criterion B) within 6 h. It also does not note that Apgar 7 at 5 min makes HIE less likely.
evidence: ACOG/AAP Neonatal Encephalopathy and Neurologic Outcome, 2nd ed 2014; BAPM therapeutic hypothermia framework 2020 (pH <7.0 or BD >= 16 within 60 min).
fix: Add: "pH below 7.00 within an hour of birth meets the first criterion for cooling. Examine for encephalopathy now and repeat; cooling must start within 6 hours. An Apgar of 7 at 5 minutes makes severe HIE less likely but does not exclude it." Add acog14/bapm20 to SRC and src.

what: 'A lactate above about 8 in smoke inhalation suggests cyanide.' The smoke-inhalation threshold is >10 mmol/L (Baud 1991: sens 87%, spec 94%, PPV 95% for blood cyanide >40 µmol/L). The 8 mmol/L cut-off comes from pure cyanide poisoning (Baud 2002). The case lactate 9.2 sits between the two, so it is a borderline example for the teaching point.
evidence: Baud FJ et al. N Engl J Med 1991;325:1761–6 (summary: https://www.medschool.umaryland.edu/em/cme/umem-educational-pearls/?id=3156).
fix: Change the case lactate to 11–12 (adjust HCO₃⁻/AG to fit) and the text to 'A lactate above 10 mmol/L in a smoke-inhalation victim strongly suggests cyanide (Baud 1991)'. Add a baud91 entry to SRC (c5.js) and to im-co src.

what: The explanation for a wrong option reads like a confirmation: 'Consistent with rhabdomyolysis; repeat only if the story does not fit.' It does not say why contamination is wrong.
evidence: Pick 'Contaminated sample' in im-dip step 1.
fix: 'Contamination (e.g. menstrual blood) brings intact red cells, which microscopy would show; 0–2/hpf means free haem pigment.'

what: The stem combines two pre-analytical errors: an air bubble (PO₂ toward ~150, PCO₂ down) and a 40-minute wait (ongoing metabolism lowers PO₂ and raises PCO₂). They push PO₂ in opposite directions; the explanation only mentions air.
evidence: Read im-print step 3.
fix: Either drop '40 minutes' or add to the explanation: 'delay alone would lower PO₂; here the bubble dominates'. Also show 'FiO₂ 21%' in the printout header (printout() hides FiO₂ when 0.21).

what: The confused smoke-inhalation patient is assessed and gassed 'on air' (fio2 0.21). In practice she is on 15 L non-rebreather oxygen from the door; the case never asks for oxygen or hyperbaric decisions, the core CO management (Weaver 2009).
evidence: im-co intro and step 2 gas (fio2:0.21).
fix: Say 'gas taken on arrival before oxygen' or put her on 15 L. Add a step 3: 'COHb 27%, confused: next?' → 100% O₂ via non-rebreather now and discuss HBO with the regional centre (Weaver 2009 criteria: loss of consciousness, neuro signs, COHb > 25%, etc.); distractor 'oxygen until SpO₂ normal' (it already is).

what: Methylene blue guidance is incomplete for a case aimed at MRCEM: no infusion time, no repeat dose, no mention of serotonergic drugs, and no fallback.
evidence: Wright 1999 (Ann Emerg Med 34:646): 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min, repeat after 1 h if needed; ineffective/harmful in G6PD deficiency; exchange transfusion/HBO if refractory.
fix: Extend: 'Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 5 min; repeat after an hour if needed. Avoid in G6PD deficiency and with serotonergic drugs; if it fails, think G6PD deficiency or sulfhaemoglobin and call toxicology (exchange transfusion).'

what: Distractors for the flat trace are weak ('hyperventilating', 'improved lung perfusion'). The real differential a clinician runs is DOPE/equipment: disconnection, blocked or kinked sampling line, ventilator failure, arrest.
evidence: Read im-capno step 2.
fix: Replace 'Improved lung perfusion' with 'Blocked sampling line: change the line and carry on' (explanation: possible, but you assume displacement until you have checked the tube); add 'Cardiac arrest' (explanation: CPR still gives a low trace; check a pulse too).

what: Exertional collapse in the heat without a temperature: exertional heat stroke is the first thing to exclude in this story and changes management (cooling).
evidence: im-dip intro.
fix: Add 'Temperature 38.1 °C (rectal 38.4 °C after 30 min of cooling)' to the intro, or a step on heat stroke.

where: im-syringe printouts A/B; ch-copd ('PCO₂ 76'); ch-cord ('PCO₂ 52 … 86'); im-co ('PaO₂ 410')
what: Case prose hard-codes mmHg numbers with no unit. In kPa mode the printout image beside it converts (Printout A reads PCO₂ 5.3 kPa) while the question says 'Printout A: pH 7.40, PCO₂ 40, HCO₃⁻ 14.', so the two contradict each other on the same screen.
evidence: Run grep -o 'PCO₂ [0-9]' c12.js: there are 7 hard-coded pressures in steps and messages.
fix: Write the pressures as tokens (e.g. '{p:40}') and render them through P()/PU() in caseStep/caseBubble, or at least add the unit ('PCO₂ 40 mmHg (5.3 kPa)').

what: The step gives glucose, ketones, pH, HCO₃⁻ and chloride but no sodium. The keyed explanation says 'The gap is closing', which the learner cannot check.
evidence: Nineteen and vomiting, step 4.
fix: Add 'Na⁺ 138' (AG 138 − 112 − 14 = 12) so the learner can see the gap close and the NAGMA appear.

where: ch-pca steps 1-2, ch-meth step 1, ch-cord step 2
what: Four steps in "chat" cases have no message at all. Step 1 of ch-pca and ch-meth opens with an empty chat and a bare question, and the PCA gas appears with no "ABG is back" bubble, which breaks the chat format.
evidence: /tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/80312b5f-0e45-5589-b131-fcf824f33899/scratchpad/beta/shots/T20-pca-gas-desk.png: only the "You" bubble above the gas.
fix: Add short messages: ch-pca step 1 Nurse: "She only groans to a sternal rub. Pupils pinpoint."; step 2 Nurse: "ABG back, on 4 L."; ch-meth step 1 Nurse: "VBG back. Glucose and lactate are on it."; ch-cord step 2 Midwife: "So is the baby acidotic?".

what: "Ketone meter says 5.8" has no units. The best option "Venous gas, then start fluids while you assess" reads as if fluids wait for the gas.
evidence: c12.js line 8.
fix: "Ketones 5.8 mmol/L". Option: "Venous gas and IV access, start 0.9% saline 1 L over an hour while you assess".

where: ch-asa step 2 distractor "Activated charcoal and observe for 12 h"
what: The feedback implies charcoal is pointless. It is the "observe" part that is wrong: charcoal still has a role in large or enteric-coated salicylate ingestions.
evidence: TOXBASE salicylate guidance (charcoal within 1 h; consider later for enteric-coated or very large doses).
fix: "Charcoal may still help, but a toxic, agitated patient at six hours needs enhanced elimination now, not observation."

where: ch-copd step 3 and ch-meth step 2 distractors
what: Weak distractors: "Discharge on home oxygen" for an acidaemic drowsy patient, and "Give bicarbonate and send him home". Nobody would pick them, so the question tests nothing.
evidence: c12.js lines 20 and 24.
fix: COPD: "Intubate and ventilate now" (feedback: NIV first unless contraindicated or failing; set a ceiling of care). Methanol: "Fomepizole alone; no dialysis needed because he is still talking" (feedback: visual signs, AG >24 and pH <= 7.15 are EXTRIP indications).

what: Base deficit is given only for sample 2, which hints at the answer. The other values (HCO3, PO2) are missing, so the gases cannot be checked.
evidence: Midwife: "Sample 1: pH 7.21, PCO2 52. Sample 2: pH 6.94, PCO2 86, base deficit 14."
fix: Show both samples as slips (gas objects with pH, PCO2, PO2, HCO3; BD computed): vein pH 7.21/PCO2 52/HCO3 ~20.6, artery 6.94/86/~18.3. Ask the learner to note the wide A-V gap (pH 0.27, PCO2 34), which suggests acute cord occlusion.

what: ch-copd and ch-pca are tagged MRCEM only, but hypercapnic failure, NIV and opioid toxicity are core USMLE Step 2 CK. ch-cord is tagged USMLE only, though MRCEM covers neonatal resuscitation.
evidence: c12.js lines 16, 25, 30.
fix: ch-copd and ch-pca: exam:['MRCEM','USMLE']. Consider adding MRCEM to ch-cord, or leave it as is if the cord-gas detail is judged out of scope.

what: 'Normal' (step 1) is a give-away distractor.
evidence: Read im-capno step 1.
fix: Replace with 'Hypoventilation' (explanation: a raised ETCO₂ keeps a square shape; this is about shape, not height) or 'Rebreathing'.

what: 'Diabetic ketoacidosis' is implausible.
evidence: Read im-co step 2.
fix: Replace with 'Carbon monoxide alone; oxygen is enough' (explanation: CO raises lactate modestly; a lactate this high with acidosis needs a cyanide antidote now). Add to the right answer: hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV, and draw co-oximetry first because hydroxocobalamin interferes with it.

what: Patient's sex is not given in the intro ('A 26-year-old'), but the explanation says 'she is comfortable'.
evidence: Read intro and step 2 option 3 explanation.
fix: 'A 26-year-old woman after dental work…'.

what: 'Room-air PaO₂ cannot exceed the alveolar PO₂ of about 100' is only true at a PCO₂ near 40 (PAO₂ = 150 − PCO₂/0.8).
evidence: Read im-print step 3.
fix: '…of about 100 at this PCO₂ (PAO₂ = 150 − 39/0.8 ≈ 101)'.

what: 'Resus 2: DKA' is listed before 'Resus 1: septic shock'.
evidence: Screenshot /tmp/claude-0/-home-claude/80312b5f-0e45-5589-b131-fcf824f33899/scratchpad/beta/shots/T30-caselib.png
fix: Reorder the CASES entries or sort sims by number.

what: Bicarbonate rose only 1.4 mmol/L/h (5.6 -> 14 in 6 h) while ketones fell 0.73/h. That is the classic trap (bicarbonate lags because of hyperchloraemia), and JBDS says not to use bicarbonate as the marker at this stage.
evidence: JBDS 2023 pathway: resolution = ketones <0.6 and pH >7.3; "bicarbonate should not be used as a marker".
fix: Add a distractor "Bicarbonate is rising too slowly; increase the insulin", with feedback on chloride and the targets (ketones fall >= 0.5/h, glucose >= 3/h).

what: Sodium 131 with glucose 31 is a chance to teach corrected sodium (~138), which matters for fluid choice and cerebral oedema risk in a 19-year-old.
fix: Add one line to the step-2 explanation or a short extra question.

what: The six cases cover HAGMA x3, respiratory acidosis x2 and neonatal. There is no NAGMA (diarrhoea or RTA), no metabolic alkalosis (pyloric stenosis, vomiting or diuretics), and no triple disorder in chat format.
evidence: CASES chat dis tags: hagma, hagma/ralk/mixed, rac, hagma, rac, mixed.
fix: Add chat cases: infant with pyloric stenosis (hypochloraemic alkalosis, paradoxical aciduria); high-output ileostomy NAGMA with urine anion gap; alcoholic with vomiting plus AKA (HAGMA + metabolic alkalosis, delta ratio > 2).

where: new image case: capnography during CPR
what: Highest-value addition: ETCO₂ during CPR. Traces: low 8–10 mmHg with poor compressions → rises to 15–20 after compressor swap → sudden jump to 40+ = ROSC; plus 'ETCO₂ <10 after 20 min'. Directly examinable (MRCEM) and used every shift.
evidence: RCUK/ERC 2021 ALS guidance on waveform capnography in CPR.
fix: capnoSVG kind 'cpr' (compression-rate small waves) and 'rosc' (step-up); 3-step case.

what: Link to im-dip (K⁺ 6.1): a rhythm strip with peaked T, then wide QRS/sine wave as K⁺ rises; questions on calcium, insulin–dextrose, and why calcium is still given in rhabdomyolysis despite later hypercalcaemia risk.
evidence: Reuse the ECG app's SVG generator if available.
fix: New img type 'ecg' with k:'peakedT'|'wideQRS'|'sine'.

what: Centrifuged tubes: pink plasma (haemoglobin, haemolysis) vs clear plasma with cola urine (myoglobin). Adds the classic discriminator to im-dip and a pseudo-hyperkalaemia case.
evidence: Bosch 2009.
fix: New img type 'tube' with plasma/urine colours.

what: Few breaths of decaying waveform then flat (NAP4: 'no trace = wrong place'), including during cardiac arrest.
evidence: Cook 2011 NAP4.
fix: capnoSVG kind 'oeso'; add to im-capno or a new case.

what: Drop of blood on white filter paper beside a normal control: brown stays brown (classic bedside test, Wright 1999). More realistic than a swatch on a black screen.
evidence: Wright 1999.
fix: Add to syringeSVG as a second panel.

what: A follow-up case where methylene blue fails (dapsone, G6PD or sulfHb) – a high-yield twist for USMLE.
evidence: Wright 1999.
fix: New image case or extra step in im-syringe.

what: (4) 16 cases cover too little for two exams and daily shift practice. There are no cases for HHS, AKA, toxic alcohol follow-up, PE, heat stroke on site (Saudi summer), CO, paediatric DKA or Hajj/Umrah heat.
evidence: Learner session, 13/11/2026
fix: Grow to about 40 cases, including local presentations (exertional heat stroke at outdoor work sites, scorpion or snakebite-related rhabdomyolysis, Ramadan fasting DKA/AKA) with MRCEM/USMLE tags.
